title: Quantum Reservoir Computing
intro: Quantum reservoir computing (QRC) uses the natural dynamics of a quantum system as a fixed, untrained recurrent network and trains only a linear readout on measured expectation values. This shelf goes from the classical theory it inherits, through the open-system maths it needs, to the models, the hardware, the measurement problem and what is and is not known about its power.

blocks.text: The symbols used across this shelf. Reservoir computing borrows letters from machine learning, dynamical systems and quantum information, so many of them have more than one meaning; every meaning is listed, numbered, with the setting it belongs to. Highlight a symbol on any page of the shelf to see its meanings. The symbols of the underlying quantum mechanics are listed on the Quantum Mechanics shelf (#/quantum).

items: $u_k,\ u(t)$: the input at step $k$ on the classical reservoir pages; $u(t)$ is an input applied as a continuous drive.
$s_k$: the input at step $k$ on the quantum pages, $s_k\in[0,1]$, because it sets a qubit amplitude.
$k$: the time step: the $k$-th input, with $\rho_k$ and $x_k$ the state and features after it.
$y_k,\ \hat y_k$: the target at step $k$; $\hat y_k$ is the readout's prediction of it.

$T,\ T_0,\ \mathcal{T}_s$: (1) the length of a time series (number of input steps); $T_0$ is the washout and $T_{\mathrm{test}}$ the number of test points; (2) $\mathcal{T}_{s}$: the input-dependent channel applied at each step, $\rho_k = \mathcal{T}_{s_k}(\rho_{k-1})$; (3) for a qubit channel: the $3\times3$ matrix in its Bloch map $\vec r\mapsto T\vec r + \vec t$; (4) in a delay reservoir: the response time of the nonlinear node.
$T_1,\ T_2,\ T_\varphi$: the pure-dephasing time, from $1/T_2 = 1/(2T_1) + 1/T_\varphi$ ($T_1$ is the relaxation time and $T_2$ the coherence time).
$\Delta t$: the time the reservoir evolves between two inputs.
$d$: (1) a delay: the memory function $r^2(d)$ scores recall of the input $d$ steps back; (2) the dimension of a Hilbert space; an input state on $d$ dimensions has $d^2$ operators.
$L,\ L_j,\ \mathcal{L}$: (1) a number of past inputs: a window of the last $L$ steps; (2) $L_j$: the jump operators of a Lindblad equation, and $\mathcal{L}$ the Liouvillian.
$w$: (1) the readout weight vector, the only thing learned; (2) the memory window: a restart only needs the last $w$ inputs.

$\tau$: (1) a delay: the $\tau = 17$ in the Mackey-Glass equation, or a delay reservoir's feedback delay ($\tau_{\mathrm{in}}$ is the time an input is held); (2) a memory time: two copies of a reservoir approach by $e^{-1/\tau}$ per step; (3) the time a Hamiltonian encoding acts, $e^{-i(H_0 + sH_1)\tau}$.
$\theta$: (1) in a delay reservoir: the spacing of virtual nodes along the delay; (2) an encoding angle, $\theta_k = 2\arcsin\sqrt{s_k}$ in $R_Y(\theta_k)$.
$\mathrm{MC}$: linear memory capacity; NMSE: mean squared error divided by the target variance (both in the glossary under their names).
$x_k$: the feature vector (reservoir state) at step $k$; $x_{k,i}$ is its $i$-th feature, $\operatorname{Tr}(O_i\rho_k)$ for a quantum reservoir.
$x,\ p$: (1) a single feature value, such as $\langle Z_i\rangle = x$ estimated from shots; (2) for an oscillator: the position quadrature, with $p$ the momentum.

$N$: (1) the number of reservoir units (features) in an echo state network; (2) for an oscillator: the Fock-space truncation, keeping levels $0$ to $N-1$; (3) $N_{\mathrm{ens}}$: the number of identical copies in an ensemble readout.

$W,\ W_{\mathrm{in}},\ W_{\mathrm{out}}$: (1) the recurrent weight matrix of an echo state network ($N\times N$, random); $W_{\mathrm{in}}$ holds the input weights and $W_{\mathrm{out}}$ the trained readout; (2) for a spin reservoir: the disorder strength, with random fields drawn from $[-W/2, W/2]$.

$\rho$: (1) the density matrix of the reservoir; $\rho_k$ is the state after input $k$ and $\rho_{01}$ a matrix element; (2) $\rho(W)$: the spectral radius of an ESN weight matrix, its largest eigenvalue modulus.
$a$: (1) the leak rate of an echo state network; (2) for an oscillator: the annihilation operator, with $[a, a^\dagger] = 1$.

$K,\ K_m$: (1) the input dimension of an echo state network, $u_k\in\mathbb{R}^K$; (2) the Kerr strength of a nonlinear oscillator, $K\,a^\dagger a\,a^\dagger a$; (3) the number of reservoirs run in parallel (spatial multiplexing); (4) $K_m$: the Kraus operators of a channel, $\rho\mapsto\sum_m K_m\rho K_m^\dagger$.

$\lambda$: (1) the ridge regularisation strength, in $(Z^\top Z + \lambda I)^{-1}$; (2) eigenvalues: $\lambda_i$ of $W$ (the spectral radius is $\max_i\vert\lambda_i\vert$) or $\lambda_k$ of the Liouvillian; (3) $\lambda_1$: the largest conditional Lyapunov exponent; the echo state property needs $\lambda_1 < 0$.

$\sigma$: (1) singular values: $\sigma_i$ of the feature matrix, and $\sigma_{\max}(W)$ the largest singular value of $W$; (2) a standard deviation or noise level: input variance $\sigma_u^2$, feature noise variance $\sigma^2$, or the width of a weak-measurement pointer; (3) a second density matrix, as in the trace distance $D(\rho, \sigma)$; (4) $\sigma^\pm$: the qubit raising and lowering operators in amplitude damping; (5) for oscillators: the covariance matrix $\sigma_{jk}$ of a Gaussian state.
$Z$: (1) the feature matrix: feature vectors stacked as rows, $Z\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times M}$; (2) the Pauli $Z$ operator; $\langle Z_i\rangle$ on each qubit is the usual set of features.
$Y$: the target matrix: targets stacked as rows to match $Z$.
$F$: (1) the reservoir map, $x_k = F(x_{k-1}, u_k)$; (2) the feature matrix in the ridge solution $w = (F^\top F + \lambda I)^{-1}F^\top y$.
$M,\ M_m$: (1) the number of features the readout uses; (2) $M_m$: measurement operators, with $\sum_m M_m^\dagger M_m = I$.

$r$: (1) $r^2(d)$: the squared correlation between the readout and the input $d$ steps back (the memory function); (2) $r_\mu = \operatorname{Tr}(P_\mu\rho)$: the Pauli coordinates of a state (its generalised Bloch vector); (3) $r_k$: the squeezing magnitude used to encode an input in an oscillator.
$C$: (1) a capacity: $C_{\mathrm{tot}}$ is the total information processing capacity and $C[z]$ the capacity for one target $z$; (2) the concurrence of a two-qubit state.

$m$: (1) in a delay reservoir: the mask values $m_1,\dots,m_N$ that set each virtual node's input weight; (2) a number of qubits an input is re-uploaded into, or of ancilla qubits; (3) a measurement outcome label, as in $M_m$ and $p_m$.
$b$: (1) random bits $b_k$ in the parity task; (2) the input-dependent shift in a state-affine reservoir, $r_k = A(s_k)r_{k-1} + b(s_k)$.
$A(s)$: the input-dependent matrix of a state-affine reservoir, $r_k = A(s_k)r_{k-1} + b(s_k)$.
$G$: a target filter, $y_k = G(s_k, s_{k-1}, \dots)$: causal, time-invariant and with fading memory.
$n,\ n_i$: (1) the number of qubits in the reservoir; (2) the order of a NARMA task (NARMA$n$) or of an $n$-bit parity; (3) in a Rydberg array: the occupation $n_i = (1 - Z_i)/2$ of atom $i$.
$S$: the number of shots per feature; shot noise falls as $1/\sqrt{S}$.
$V,\ V_{ij}$: (1) the number of virtual nodes: the times the reservoir is read between two inputs; (2) in a Rydberg array: the van der Waals interaction $V_{ij}\propto 1/r_{ij}^6$.

$O_i,\ O_w,\ O(\cdot)$: (1) $O_i$: the observables read out, so feature $i$ is $\operatorname{Tr}(O_i\rho_k)$; (2) $O_w = \sum_k w_kE_k$: the single observable a trained QELM readout amounts to; (3) $O(\cdot)$: order of growth, as in a cost of $O(ST^2)$.

$E_m,\ E_k,\ \mathcal{E}$: (1) $E_m$: POVM elements, $E_m = M_m^\dagger M_m$, with $p_m = \operatorname{Tr}(E_m\rho)$; (2) $E_k$: an effective POVM, the measurement pulled back through the reservoir, $E_k = \mathcal{E}^\dagger(\Pi_k)$; (3) $E_k$: energy levels, whose gaps give the level statistics; (4) $\mathcal{E}$: a quantum channel.
$J,\ J_{ij}$: (1) the couplings $J_{ij}$ of a spin reservoir, drawn at scale $J$; (2) $J_k$: the Jacobian of the driven map at step $k$; (3) $J(\mathcal{E})$: the Choi matrix of a channel.
$h,\ h_i$: the field on each qubit of a spin reservoir, $h_i = h + \delta_i$.

$\delta$: (1) $\delta_i$: the random offsets of the fields in a disordered spin reservoir; (2) a detuning between two spins, $\delta = h_1 - h_2$, which limits how far an excitation hops; (3) a failure probability: all estimates are within $\epsilon$ with probability $1-\delta$.

$\Delta$: (1) in a Rydberg array: the detunings $\Delta_i$; (2) $\Delta(\rho)$: the map that removes all coherences in the computational basis (full dephasing); (3) for an oscillator: the detuning in $\Delta\,a^\dagger a$.
$\Omega$: in a Rydberg array: the Rabi drive on each atom.

$\gamma$: (1) a decay rate: amplitude damping at $\gamma = 1/T_1$, or the rate $\gamma_j$ of jump operator $L_j$; (2) the amplitude-damping probability per step in a channel's Kraus form; (3) the decay coefficient in the Mackey-Glass equation.
$\kappa$: the photon-loss rate of an oscillator.
$\eta$: (1) the contraction coefficient of a channel: the most it can keep the trace distance between two states; (2) noise added to the features, of variance $\sigma^2$.

$\epsilon,\ \varepsilon$: (1) a target precision: the number of shots grows as $\epsilon^{-2}$; (2) the strength of a weak measurement, from $0$ (nothing learned) to $1$ (projective); (3) the input drive amplitude of an oscillator reservoir.
$\alpha$: (1) the input scaling of the drive in a Kerr oscillator reservoir, $\alpha\,u(t)(a + a^\dagger)$; (2) the amplitude of a coherent state $\vert\alpha\rangle$.
$\beta$: the feedback coefficient in the Mackey-Glass equation.
$\mu$: an index over Pauli strings, as in $\rho = 2^{-n}(I + \sum_\mu r_\mu P_\mu)$.

$p$: (1) the strength of depolarising noise per step, $\rho\mapsto(1-p)\rho + pI/2^n$; (2) a probability: $p_m$ or $p_k$ of a measurement outcome; (3) the exponent $p = 10$ in the Mackey-Glass equation.
$D$: (1) the trace distance $D(\rho, \sigma) = \tfrac12\Vert\rho - \sigma\Vert_1$; (2) the Hilbert-space dimension $D = 2^n$; $I/D$ is the maximally mixed state.
$g$: (1) the Liouvillian gap: the slowest rate at which the state approaches its steady state; (2) $g_k = E_{k+1} - E_k$: the gaps between neighbouring energy levels.
$P_\mu,\ P_n$: (1) $P_\mu$: a Pauli string; (2) $P_n$: the population of Fock state $\vert n\rangle$.
$U$: (1) the unitary applied in one reservoir step; (2) $\mathcal{U}[a, b]$: the uniform distribution on $[a, b]$, used to draw random couplings.
$\Pi$: (1) the parity $\Pi = Z_1Z_2\cdots Z_n$, conserved by the spin-network reservoir; (2) $\Pi_m$: projectors of a projective measurement.
$I$: the identity; $I/D$ (or $I/2^n$) is the maximally mixed state.
$c$: the contraction factor per step: distances shrink as $c^k$, so $c^{d_{\max}}$ should be small for the longest delay needed.
$\phi_k$: the squeezing phase used to encode an input in an oscillator.

blocks.text: A recurrent network has to be trained through time, which is slow and unstable. Reservoir computing (Jaeger's echo state networks and Maass's liquid state machines, both 2001–2002) separates the job: a fixed, randomly built dynamical system (the reservoir) is driven by the input, its state becomes a rich nonlinear record of the recent input history, and only a linear readout is trained, by ridge regression in one shot. Anything with the right dynamics can be the reservoir: a bucket of water, a laser with delayed feedback, a spintronic oscillator. Fujii and Nakajima (2017) proposed a quantum one: a register of interacting qubits whose Hilbert space grows as $2^n$, read out through expectation values.

blocks.caption: The whole of QRC: a quantum channel that depends on the input drives the state; measured expectations are the features; only the linear readout w is trained.

blocks.text: For this to work as a reservoir the input-driven channel must forget its initial state (the echo state property, which in the quantum case requires the input-driven channels to contract the distance between states, at least over several steps, so a closed unitary system alone never qualifies); it must mix past inputs nonlinearly; and the features must be estimated from a finite number of measurement shots, each of which disturbs or destroys the state. Those three facts organise most of the field.

items: Reservoir Computing Foundations (#/qrc/foundations): echo state networks, the echo state property and fading memory, memory capacity and information processing capacity, physical reservoirs, and the benchmark tasks every QRC paper reports.

Open Quantum Systems Toolkit (#/qrc/open-systems): density matrices, channels and Kraus operators, Lindblad dynamics, contraction and fixed points, and generalised measurement: the quantum mechanics past the basics that QRC runs on.

Quantum Reservoir Models (#/qrc/models): the transverse-field spin reservoir, input encodings, readouts and multiplexing, ergodic and localised regimes, dissipation as a resource, continuous-variable reservoirs, quantum extreme learning machines and tasks on quantum data.

Measurement and Hardware (#/qrc/hardware): measurement back-action and its cost, online protocols (weak, repeated and mid-circuit measurement), gate-based and analog platforms, and an honest count of shots and time.

Theory, Limits and Practice (#/qrc/theory): expressivity and universality, exponential concentration and scalability, where quantum advantage could and could not come from, a complete runnable implementation, and open problems.

blocks.text: New to quantum mechanics? Start with the Quantum Mechanics shelf (#/quantum): it covers the states, measurement, qubits, time evolution, entanglement and mixed states these pages assume, in the same notation, and every page there links back to the QRC pages that use it.

items: If reservoir computing is new: Echo State Networks (#/qrc/foundations/echo-state-networks), then The Echo State Property (#/qrc/foundations/echo-state-property) and Memory and Capacity (#/qrc/foundations/memory-and-capacity).

Then the quantum tools: Density Matrices and Channels (#/qrc/open-systems/density-matrices-and-channels) and Contraction and Fixed Points (#/qrc/open-systems/contraction-and-fixed-points) (this is where the echo state property becomes a statement about channels).

Then the reference model, with the live simulator: The Spin-Network Reservoir (#/qrc/models/spin-network-reservoir), Input Encoding (#/qrc/models/input-encoding) and Readout and Multiplexing (#/qrc/models/readout-and-multiplexing).
Then the reality check: Measurement Back-Action (#/qrc/hardware/measurement-back-action) and Concentration and Scalability (#/qrc/theory/concentration-and-scalability).
Finally, build one yourself: Hands-On Implementation (#/qrc/theory/hands-on-implementation).

blocks.text: The interactive plots on this shelf run an exact density-matrix simulation of a 2- to 5-qubit reservoir in your browser, so every number they show comes from the real model, not a sketch.
